title: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus: immune evasion, therapeutic landscape, and vaccine prospects
abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) is an emerging tick-borne bunyavirus that poses a growing public health threat. National surveillance data from China (2010-2023) report an overall case fatality rate of approximately 4.8%. However, hospital-based cohorts of severe or critically ill patients report substantially higher rates, ranging from 12% to 30%. Despite its designation as a WHO priority pathogen in 2017, no vaccine has been approved, although a first-in-human Phase I/II trial of an mRNA vaccine candidate was initiated in 2025, and favipiravir, the only authorized antiviral (Japan, 2024), remains of debated clinical benefit, leaving a widening gap between mechanistic understanding and clinical translation. This gap is rooted in the virus’s ability to dismantle the very immune pathways on which vaccines and antivirals depend. The non-structural protein NSs sequesters TBK1, IRF3, and STAT1/STAT2 into viroplasm-like structures, while the nucleoprotein NP induces autophagy-mediated degradation of cGAS and MAVS, collectively diminishing type I interferon responses, impairing B-cell and T-cell immunity, and permitting the dysregulated cytokine storm that is associated with multi-organ failure. These same mechanisms explain why vaccine candidates that perform well in immunocompromised (IFNAR−/− or STAT2−/−) mouse models have not translated to immunocompetent or aged populations, and why antiviral efficacy collapses at high viral loads or late treatment initiation. Unlike prior reviews that treat pathogenesis, antivirals, and vaccines as separate topics, this review integrates them into a single framework linking viral immune evasion to the failure modes of current countermeasures, and identifies the specific obstacles that must be overcome before clinical translation: missing correlates of protection, immunocompromised animal models, and reassortment-driven antigenic diversity. We conclude by outlining priority directions, including AI-assisted antigen design, host-directed and combination therapies, standardized animal models, and integrated One Health surveillance.

title: Explainable machine learning integrating virological and immune-inflammatory biomarkers for in-hospital mortality prediction in severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome
abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), characterized by an excessive inflammatory response and impaired adaptive immunity, is associated with a high risk of mortality. This study aims to establish and validate a machine learning (ML)-based predictive model integrating clinical and immune-inflammatory biomarkers for in-hospital mortality in patients with SFTS. A total of 238 patients, including 177 survivors and 61 non-survivors, were divided by stratified random sampling into a training cohort ( n = 167) and an internal validation cohort ( n = 71) at a 7:3 ratio. Features were selected from the intersection of Boruta, Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO), and random forest recursive feature elimination (RF-RFE). Model hyperparameters were optimized exclusively within the training cohort using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation, with the internal validation cohort reserved for final evaluation. Model performance was then assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration plots, and decision curve analysis (DCA). SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) was employed to improve model interpretability. To facilitate individualized risk estimation, the selected model was presented as a nomogram and incorporated into an interactive web-based calculator. The final logistic regression model incorporated four predictors: SFTSV RNA load, CD3+CD4+ T-cell count, IL-6, and PCT. In the internal validation cohort, the area under the ROC curve was 0.841 (95% CI: 0.736–0.930). Based on the maximum Youden index in the training cohort, the optimal cutoff probability was established at 0.2053. When this cutoff was applied to the validation cohort, the model yielded a sensitivity of 0.944 (95% CI: 0.742–0.990) and specificity of 0.698 (95% CI: 0.565–0.805). The model also demonstrated a Brier score of 0.139 (95% CI: 0.094–0.189) and potential net clinical benefit. We present an interpretable predictive model based on viral, immune, and inflammatory biomarkers for predicting in-hospital mortality in patients with SFTS. A multicenter prospective evaluation is highly recommended prior to its clinical use.

source_body_en: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), characterized by an excessive inflammatory response and impaired adaptive immunity, is associated with a high risk of mortality. This study aims to establish and validate a machine learning (ML)-based predictive model integrating clinical and immune-inflammatory biomarkers for in-hospital mortality in patients with SFTS. A total of 238 patients, including 177 survivors and 61 non-survivors, were divided by stratified random sampling into a training cohort ( n = 167) and an internal validation cohort ( n = 71) at a 7:3 ratio. Features were selected from the intersection of Boruta, Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO), and random forest recursive feature elimination (RF-RFE). Model hyperparameters were optimized exclusively within the training cohort using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation, with the internal validation cohort reserved for final evaluation. Model performance was then assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration plots, and decision curve analysis (DCA). SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) was employed to improve model interpretability. To facilitate individualized risk estimation, the selected model was presented as a nomogram and incorporated into an interactive web-based calculator. The final logistic regression model incorporated four predictors: SFTSV RNA load, CD3+CD4+ T-cell count, IL-6, and PCT. In the internal validation cohort, the area under the ROC curve was 0.841 (95% CI: 0.736–0.930). Based on the maximum Youden index in the training cohort, the optimal cutoff probability was established at 0.2053. When this cutoff was applied to the validation cohort, the model yielded a sensitivity of 0.944 (95% CI: 0.742–0.990) and specificity of 0.698 (95% CI: 0.565–0.805). The model also demonstrated a Brier score of 0.139 (95% CI: 0.094–0.189) and potential net clinical benefit. We present an interpretable predictive model based on viral, immune, and inflammatory biomarkers for predicting in-hospital mortality in patients with SFTS. A multicenter prospective evaluation is highly recommended prior to its clinical use.

title: Epidemiological characteristics and recorded case fatality across prevention and control phases of SFTS in Changqing District, China, 2020–2025
abstract: Objective This study aims to analyze the epidemiological characteristics, clinical diagnosis and treatment delays, and temporal changes in recorded case fatality and Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) -related knowledge across prevention and control phases for SFTS in Changqing District, Jinan City, from 2020 to 2025. The findings may inform local SFTS surveillance and prevention planning. Methods Data were collected from 119 laboratory-confirmed SFTS cases recorded between January 2020 and December 2025 in the Changqing District SFTS surveillance database, which was derived from the China National Notifiable Infectious Disease Surveillance System (NNIDSS). Descriptive epidemiological methods were employed to analyze temporal, spatial, and population distribution patterns. Additionally, questionnaire surveys evaluated changes in awareness of prevention measures among residents and healthcare workers before and after implementation of interventions. Annual and phase-specific CFRs were calculated with Wilson 95% confidence intervals. Recorded CFRs were compared across phases using the two-sided Fisher–Freeman–Halton exact test, and an exact ordinal trend test assessed trends across the three ordered phases. Unadjusted risk differences and risk ratios were reported with 95% confidence intervals. Annual incidence and recorded mortality trends were assessed using population-offset Poisson models, with assessment of overdispersion. Results The mean annual incidence rate was 3.27 per 100,000 population, with annual rates ranging from 1.50 to 4.74 per 100,000. Cases were reported from all townships and subdistricts. The highest estimated mean annual incidence rates were observed in Mashan Town (15.92 per 100,000), Shuangquan Town (12.57 per 100,000), and Xiaoli Town (8.68 per 100,000). Among recorded cases, the largest age group was 60–69 years (40.34%), and 86.55% were farmers (103/119). The median duration from symptom onset to diagnosis was 7 days, compared with a median interval of 1 day from symptom onset to first medical consultation. A substantial 61.34% of patients initially sought care at village clinics or township health centers. Annual recorded CFRs ranged from 6.90% (95% CI: 1.91%–21.96%) to 33.33% (95% CI: 12.06%–64.58%). Phase-specific recorded CFRs were 22.22%, 8.70%, and 20.83%, respectively, with no statistically significant difference among phases ( P = 0.416). The percentage of correct responses in the basic knowledge domain increased from 43.0% to 94.0% among residents and from 76.0% to 100.0% among healthcare workers between the pre-early-screening and comprehensive prevention and control phases. Conclusion Recorded SFTS cases in Changqing District showed geographical variation in estimated incidence, with farmers accounting for most cases and adults aged 60–69 years comprising the largest age group. Delays between symptom onset and diagnosis were observed. Recorded CFRs did not show a statistically significant or sustained decline across the prevention and control phases. These descriptive findings may inform surveillance and prevention planning.

title: Burden of small-mammal-associated zoonoses in north-east Asia: A systematic review
abstract: Small-mammal-associated zoonoses such as haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, scrub typhus, leptospirosis and severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome are common notifiable infections in north-east Asia, but their burden in the region is poorly understood. Human cases are counted by separate surveillance systems with different case definitions, while infection in the small mammals and ectoparasites that maintain these pathogens is reported in a largely separate literature. The two are rarely measured in the same place and period, and the inputs a burden estimate needs are not reported consistently. This systematic review brings the two together for pathogens grouped into five transmission guilds. For the Republic of Korea, we extract all reported human, host and vector estimates for the four guilds other than flea-borne pathogens, and pool prevalence where studies are comparable. For the rest of north-east Asia (China, Japan, Mongolia, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, Taiwan and the Russian Far East), we map the available evidence for all five guilds without pooling. For each pathogen and country or area, we record which burden inputs are reported and which are missing. We also describe studies that measured infection in animals and disease in people in the same area. The expected outputs are pooled prevalence estimates for the Republic of Korea, an evidence map for the rest of the region, an inventory of missing burden inputs, and a minimum set of reporting items for future studies. The review is a first step towards a regional burden estimate.

full_text: Abstract Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), caused by Dabie bandavirus, carries a case fatality rate of 12–30%. In a retrospective cohort of 120 SFTS patients (4 asymptomatic, 70 mild, 26 moderate, 20 severe), 17 (14.2%) had critical illness, of whom 11 died in-hospital (9.2%). Admission interleukin-6 (IL-6) rose across severity grades (mild 9.1, moderate 12.6, severe 61.4 pg/mL; p < 0.001) and was higher in critical illness than non-critical illness (99.4 vs. 10.0 pg/mL; p < 0.001). Critical illness patients had lower initial CD4 + T-cell counts (167 vs. 420 cells/μL; n = 63; p = 0.036) and a lower one-week CD4/CD8 ratio (0.5 vs. 1.6; n = 24; p = 0.0004). Initial viral load was higher in critical illness (143,948 vs. 40,059 copies/mL; p = 0.047) but not at one week (p = 0.167), suggesting that initial viral burden, rather than delayed clearance, is associated with critical illness. Mixed-effects models showed different lymphocyte-fraction and platelet trajectories by outcome. Admission IL-6 (cutoff 18.9 pg/mL) discriminated severe disease (AUC 0.890; cross-validated) and improved an exploratory multivariable model (p = 0.004), although its adjusted odds ratio was not significant (p = 0.22). These confirmatory findings are integrated into a two-axis model that is hypothesis-generating pending external validation. analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 120 SFTS patients, stratified into asymptomatic, mild, moderate, and severe categories, with 17 patients experiencing critical illness.
analysis.methods: The study used mixed-effects models to analyze lymphocyte-fraction and platelet trajectories by outcome, and assessed admission IL-6 levels as a discriminatory marker.

analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that initial viral burden, rather than delayed clearance, is associated with critical illness, and that IL-6 levels may serve as a biomarker for severe disease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results may inform the development of targeted diagnostic tools and therapeutic strategies for SFTS, particularly in identifying patients at risk of critical illness.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the immune response and interleukin-6 (IL-6) dynamics in severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) to identify factors linked to critical illness and mortality. A retrospective cohort of 120 SFTS patients was stratified by disease severity, revealing that 14.2% experienced critical illness, with 9.2% dying in-hospital. Admission IL-6 levels were significantly higher in severe cases, and critical illness patients had lower initial CD4 + T-cell counts and a reduced CD4/CD8 ratio. Mixed-effects models showed distinct lymphocyte and platelet trajectories by outcome, and IL-6 was found to be a potential biomarker for severe disease. Abstract Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), caused by Dabie bandavirus, carries a case fatality rate of 12–30%. In a retrospective cohort of 120 SFTS patients (4 asymptomatic, 70 mild, 26 moderate, 20 severe), 17 (14.2%) had critical illness, of whom 11 died in-hospital (9.2%). Admission interleukin-6 (IL-6) rose across severity grades (mild 9.1, moderate 12.6, severe 61.4 pg/mL; p < 0.001) and was higher in critical illness than non-critical illness (99.4 vs. 10.0 pg/mL; p < 0.001). Critical illness patients had lower initial CD4 + T-cell counts (167 vs. 420 cells/μL; n = 63; p = 0.036) and a lower one-week CD4/CD8 ratio (0.5 vs. 1.6; n = 24; p = 0.0004). Initial viral load was higher in critical illness (143,948 vs. 40,059 copies/mL; p = 0.047) but not at one week (p = 0.167), suggesting that initial viral burden, rather than delayed clearance, is associated with critical illness. Mixed-effects models showed different lymphocyte-fraction and platelet trajectories by outcome.
